stage1.probe_response:
Several noteworthy aspects of the environment and task parameters will influence your approach:

• Small, Scattered Shards in Grout Lines: The leftover glass fragments are very small, and some are lodged in the tile’s grout lines. This makes them more difficult to detect and remove with a single pass of a standard tool. Their size also increases the risk of leaving behind hazardous pieces if not thoroughly collected.

• Physical Floor Characteristics: The tile surface is relatively smooth, but grout lines create irregularities. Shards can easily become partially embedded in the grout, so a method of extraction (e.g., suction or bristles) must be strong or fine enough to lift them out from crevices.

• Tool Constraints:  
  – The vacuum-like device (tool_D) is relatively heavy (3.2 kg) and requires a firm grip (28.5 N), but its suction force per particle peaks at only 0.3 N. Small, flat shards could cling to the tile or grout, potentially surpassing that suction threshold.  
  – The broom-like tool (tool_E) has bristles spaced at 1.2 mm, so very small shards (< 0.5 mm) might slip through. Relying on it exclusively risks re-distributing micro shards rather than removing them.  

• Mobility and Robot Constraints: Maneuvering a heavier device or carefully angling a bristle tool against the floor requires precise robot positioning, potentially in tight spaces around countertops or appliances in a kitchen.

• Safety and Completeness: Unlike cleaning up a larger, more visible mess, micro glass shards may be missed if you rely only on cursory sweeping or vacuuming. Thoroughness is critical to avoid leaving dangerous fragments behind in a high-traffic area.  

All of these factors combine to create a situation in which simply sweeping might not be enough, and relying solely on vacuum suction could be insufficient unless the robot experiments with angles, pressure, or repeated passes. The presence of grout lines, the risk of leaving sharp micro shards behind, and the practical limits of the available tools are what make this cleanup task uniquely challenging.

tool_selection.full_response:
(1) The main physical principle is that very small, possibly sharp glass shards are best collected by suction rather than brushing or manual pickup. Sweeping can leave behind particles smaller than the bristle gap, whereas vacuum suction applies force around each shard to pull it in.

(2) I select tool_D (the mechanical vacuum-like device).

(3) From exploration:
• tool_D has a max suction force of 0.3 N per particle—enough to pull in micro shards without leaving them behind.  
• The bristle spacing of tool_E (1.2 mm) would allow shards <0.5 mm to slip through, making it less effective.

(4) Action Plan:
• NAVIGATE_TO[kitchen_floor, spill_area] — move to the spill area with tool_D.  
• GRASP[tool_D] — ensure a firm hold with ~28.5 N grip force.  
• NEW_ACTION[vacuum_up, tool_D, spill_area]: “Use the nozzle of tool_D to create suction over the spill area and collect micro shards.”  
• RELEASE[] — set tool_D down when finished.
